newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenian shares slip, seen shackled.
newsitem.headline: Slovenian shares slip, seen shackled.

text.p: Slovenian shares eased 0.14 percent on Friday and traders said the market was likely to tread water over the next few weeks as domestic investors continued to eye the return of foreign capital.
"In the next week shares could move up or down by a maximum two to three percent and the status quo could last for another two weeks," said Andrej Obed, a trader of "A" banka.
But brokers said the market was prone to downward pressure in the long term if international investors continued to huddle on the sidelines.
In February the Bank of Slovenia blocked foreign buying by saying international investors have to open custodian accounts at Slovenian banks in order to trade in securities.
Foreign investors have criticised the costs of running such accounts as too high. Banks said costs would be about 12 percent of the amount handled.
Traders recommend buying shares of companies that had exceptionally good business results in 1996, like food maker Droga, banks Dolenjska banka, Probanka and SKB and drug firms Krka and Lek.
The blue-chip SBI index eased 1.86 points to 1,334.6 to end the week 1.2 percent lower.
Seven shares fell, eight rose, while 12 were untraded. Turnover eased to 47.5 million tolars from 67.2 million.
Health resort operator and mineral water producer Radenska was the most actively traded, firming 0.31 percent to 1,928 tolars on volume of 12,895 shares.
Pharmaceutical wholesaler Salus was the leading decliner, slumping 10.55 percent to 15,000 on volume of 200 shares.
"In spite of Salus's good business results, its shares could fall further because the court case regarding its 1990 privatisation process is not over yet," a trader said.
Last year the Payment Agency accused Salus of conducting an irregular privatisation.
Financial consultancy Primofin was the top gainer, up 5.76 percent to 14,700 on volume of 24 shares.
